approach_variants.name: Silver Falls loop from the Ohanapecosh side
approach_variants.notes:
This is a single roadside boulder at about 1,900 ft in old forest, not an alpine objective, and the approach is a walk on maintained trail with essentially no gain.

From the Ohanapecosh day-use area, follow the Silver Falls Loop about a mile. The loop can also be picked up from the Grove of the Patriarchs end via the Eastside Trail, which is the alternative when work on the campground side has closed the near entrance — that corridor has been under reconstruction in recent seasons, so check which end of the loop is open rather than assuming either.

The road serving this corner of the park is seasonal: normally open from late spring through fall and gated in winter.

No climbing permit is involved. The park's climbing permit and its blue-bag rules apply to parties travelling on glaciers or above 10,000 ft, which this is not; the park entrance fee still applies.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late spring through fall, whenever the southeast corner of the park is open to vehicles
hazards: Nothing alpine — the real risks are trail closures and construction in this corner of the park
Landing on forest floor with roots and uneven ground
Seasonal road closure to the southeast entrance in winter
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The test is that you never leave the trail. The boulder sits a few feet off the Silver Falls Loop, roughly a mile round from the Ohanapecosh day-use area. If you have stepped off maintained tread, started bushwhacking, or gained more than about a hundred feet, you have walked past it — go back rather than searching uphill.

The shape is the name: a low boulder with a loaf-shaped top hold, climbed on its left side. One problem, a couple of moves.

The strongest negative is about the whole outing rather than the last hundred yards, and it is worth stating because this route is filed under the mountain: if you are on snow, on a glacier, or anywhere above a few thousand feet, you are not near this boulder and never will be. It is in low forest in the southeast corner of the park, tens of miles and twelve thousand feet from the summit routes filed beside it.

Water and escape are non-problems here — the loop has running water nearby and you can walk out either way round it. That is the honest description; do not carry mountain planning onto it.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack cable car and Brush Creek to Whatcom Pass, then onto the Whatcom Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at about 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, FR-32, off the Mt. Baker Highway, Trail #674 runs 4.2-4.6 miles and about 2,000 ft alongside Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, the last easy reliable water before dropping into the national park.

From the pass, descend the Chilliwack River Trail through long viewless switchbacks, losing roughly 2,800 ft, past Boundary and Copper Creek camps. The river is crossed via a hand-pulled cable car near US Cabin Camp rather than a ford, which is the practical difference between this and the Easy Ridge approach.

Continue up-valley on the Brush Creek Trail toward Graybeal Camp, roughly 14 trail miles and a cumulative 4,400 ft of gain from the trailhead. The small creek near Graybeal is unreliable and can run dry by late summer, so fill earlier at the Chilliwack or US Cabin Camp. Past Graybeal the maintained tread gives way to a steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path gaining roughly 2,000 ft over the final 3 miles to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, passing Whatcom Camp and the first real views of the Challenger Glacier.
hazards: Crevasses and moats on the Whatcom Glacier, deteriorating to bare ice with gaping moats later in the season
A steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path above Graybeal Camp
The creek near Graybeal can run dry by late summer
An exposed class 3 summit ridge on poor rock
A glacier that is more open on the descent than on the ascent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route's own ground is the glacier, and you are on it as soon as you leave Whatcom Pass. From the pass, leave the trail and climb and contour south and east to gain the Whatcom Glacier at roughly 5,200-5,500 ft, then rope up and travel toward Perfect Pass, the notch and saddle south of the peak.

So the discriminator against the other two routes on this peak is the first move out of Whatcom Pass, and it is three-way: south and up the crest is the North Ridge. South and east onto ice at 5,200-5,500 ft is this route. Nothing from Whatcom Pass is the South Spur, which is approached from Easy Ridge on the other side.

Arrival at the climbing proper: from the glacier's high point near Perfect Pass, the route ascends the broad south-facing snowfield below the summit and finishes on an exposed but moderate class 3 scramble along the south ridge crest. The snowfield is the same one the South Spur uses. The two routes share their last hour and differ entirely in everything before it.

What the glacier does through the season, which is the real variable: crevasses and moats open as the year goes on and the surface can go from soft neve early to bare, polished ice with exposed water channels by mid to late summer. On the descent they are typically more open than on the way up as the afternoon sun softens the snowpack, so budget time for careful navigation rather than a quick glissade.

An alternate exit worth knowing before you need it: if the summit notch is badly melted out and choss-prone, a descent drops about 200 ft north of Peak 7347 to reach the Wiley Glacier instead of reversing through the notch.
